titre: Nag Hammadi (1945): The Jar, the Jinn, the Oven, and a Story That Shifts
accroche: The codices are real. The story of their discovery exists in at least three versions that do not agree on the number of witnesses.
contenu_vulgarise:
In almost every account of the discovery of the Nag Hammadi codices, the same scene recurs: in late 1945, an Egyptian peasant digs near a cliff to gather a natural fertilizer, hesitates, out of superstition, over a jinn, breaks open a jar, finds leather-bound papyrus books inside, and his mother burns some of them to light her oven. A blood feud is added to the mix. It is effective. But this story is not the same from one publication to the next.

## A Story That Changes From One Version to the Next

The codices themselves are quite real: twelve leather-bound papyrus codices and part of a thirteenth, in Coptic, gathering some fifty treatises, now held in the Coptic Museum in Cairo. They were copied in the 3rd and 4th centuries. What varies is the story of their discovery: who was there, who dug, who saw the jar first, and how many people witnessed the scene.

The best-known account is the one James M. Robinson, editor of *The Nag Hammadi Library*, published beginning in 1977, based on an interview with the discoverer, Muhammad Ali. In the 1977 version, only two people are at the foot of the cliff. In the 1979 one, there are seven. In the 1981 one, there are eight. The account also varies on who found the jar first.

In 1984, Rodolphe Kasser and Martin Krause cast doubt on his accounts. In 1987, a Channel 4 series, *The Gnostics*, gave the floor to Muhammad Ali himself, his only known filmed appearance: his testimony bolsters this skepticism. In a 2013 article in the *Journal for the Study of the New Testament*, Mark Goodacre concludes that Jean Doresse's 1958 account appears more trustworthy than Robinson's later, embellished versions.

## What This Changes

The texts of Nag Hammadi are safe from this doubt: they exist, and you can read them. But the setting they were given, the jar, the jinn, the oven, served for decades as an opening for books and lectures. A more detailed account is not more reliable than a short one: it is only easier to remember.

There remains a question that the good story eclipses: who, in the 4th century, copied these books, and why were they buried?

repere.texte: Robinson published three versions of the discovery: two people on the scene in 1977, seven in 1979, eight in 1981. Kasser and Krause questioned these accounts in 1984. Muhammad Ali's filmed testimony in 1987 bolsters this skepticism. In 2013 Goodacre judges Doresse's account (1958) more trustworthy.
repere.source: Mark Goodacre, “How Reliable Is the Story of the Nag Hammadi Discovery?”, JSNT 35(4), 2013

carte.punch: The discovery of Nag Hammadi: two witnesses in 1977, seven in 1979, eight in 1981.
carte.idee: The Coptic codices of Nag Hammadi are authentic. But the canonical story of their discovery, with a jinn and a blood feud, has changed from one publication to the next: two people on the scene in 1977, seven in 1979, eight in 1981. Goodacre urges caution.

quiz.question: Why does Goodacre urge caution about the story of the Nag Hammadi discovery?
choix: The codices were fabricated in the 20th century by forgers for the antiquities market
The story exists in several versions that diverge, for example on the number of people present
None of the codices was ever kept in Egypt; they all left the country as early as 1946
Muhammad Ali never agreed to be interviewed by a researcher or by a television crew
quiz.explication: Robinson's three versions count two, then seven, then eight people, and the filmed testimony of 1987 bolsters the skepticism of Kasser and Krause. The codices, for their part, are authentic and held in Cairo, and Muhammad Ali was indeed interviewed, notably in 1987.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where are the Nag Hammadi codices held today?
choix: In the Coptic Museum in Cairo
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The codices are held in the Coptic Museum in Cairo.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what language are the codices copied?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: These are texts copied in Coptic, the language of the Christians of Egypt.
